description: It is an interdisciplinary team with backgrounds in life sciences, biotechnology, and agriculture. We aim to explore how NASA data and technology can support climate resilient farming. We welcome members skilled in programming, data analysis, GIS, remote sensing, environmental science, and app or web development.
summary: Field Shift is a free web tool that helps farmers decide which crops to grow over the next two years. The farmer taps their field on a map, and Field Shift loads NASA POWER climate data for that exact point: temperature, rainfall, sunlight and root-zone moisture. The farmer then adds soil type, pH, salt, organic matter and available irrigation water, and sets what matters most: saving water, healthier soil, income, safety from heat and drought, or fodder for animals. Field Shift turns the NASA data into month-by-month crop water needs and heat risk, then ranks 20 realistic two-year crop plans for Punjab against what the farmer grows now. For a typical loam field in Sahiwal, the best plans need 560 to 690 mm less irrigation a year than rice and wheat, and lift the soil-health score from 28 to over 70. This matters because Punjab's groundwater is falling, Sahiwal gets only about 293 mm of rain in an average year, and most farmers grow the same two cereals every year on tired soil.
details:
What it does

Field Shift answers one question for a farmer: which crop plan suits my field best? It works in three steps. (1) Your farm: tap the map or pick a district, and NASA climate data for that point loads in a few seconds. (2) Soil and water: choose soil type, pH, salt, organic matter, irrigation water and tube-well quality, and say what you grow now. (3) What matters to you: five sliders for saving water, healthier soil, income, safety from heat and drought, and fodder for animals.

Field Shift then shows the best plan for the field, with the water it saves and the change in soil health compared with what the farmer grows now; all 20 plans ranked, each with five 0 to 100 scores and a 24-month crop calendar; plain-language notes such as free nitrogen from pulses (shown as bags of urea saved), heat warnings for sensitive crop stages, crops that don't suit the soil, and late sowing; a month-by-month water chart showing how much rain covers and how much must come from irrigation; the farm's NASA climate (average rain, driest and wettest years since 2001, hottest month, root-zone moisture); and a "hotter future" test that adds 1 or 2 °C.

How it works

The app calls the NASA POWER API from the browser for the chosen point, using long-term monthly averages plus monthly records from 2001 to 2024. Daily water loss from a field (reference evapotranspiration, ET0) is calculated from NASA temperature and sunlight with the Hargreaves radiation method: ET0 = 0.0135 x (T + 17.8) x Rs / 2.45. FAO-56 crop coefficients turn this into each crop's monthly water use, and usable rain (70% of NASA rainfall, up to the crop's need) is subtracted to give the irrigation needed. Rice gets an extra allowance for water lost from puddled fields. NASA monthly temperatures are compared with each crop's danger temperature at sensitive stages, such as wheat grain filling in March and April, cotton flowering in July and August, and potato planting in October and November. Soil type, pH, salt and tube-well water quality change how well each crop is expected to grow. Pulses, berseem, green manure, crop variety and residues raise the soil-health score; puddled rice, potato tillage and cereal after cereal lower it. The five scores are combined using the farmer's own slider settings. If the NASA server can't be reached, the app uses saved NASA data for Sahiwal.

Benefits and impact

In our Sahiwal example the best plans use 560 to 690 mm less irrigation a year than rice and wheat, about 5,600 to 6,900 cubic metres per hectare. Pulses and clover add nitrogen and save about 1 to 1.5 bags of urea per hectare a year. Heat warnings and the hotter-future test lower climate risk. Plans like sorghum and berseem, then maize and oats, give dairy farms green fodder all year (Sahiwal is home to the Sahiwal cattle breed). The tool is free, needs no login or install, works on a phone and shows crop names in English and Urdu.

Creativity and next steps

Instead of a single crop recommendation, Field Shift lets farmers compare whole two-year rotations against their own current practice, weighted by their own priorities. Next we want to pilot it with extension officers and dairy farmers around Sahiwal, add NASA SMAP soil moisture and Landsat/MODIS images to detect each field's real crop history, build an Urdu and Punjabi voice version, and add market prices.

Tools used

HTML, CSS and JavaScript (single web page, no server), Leaflet with OpenStreetMap, Chart.js, the NASA POWER API, FAO-56 crop coefficients, and GitHub Pages for hosting.
